candidate_texts.stem: A Schedule II prescription is issued for a resident of a long-term-care facility and is being partially filled under the federal LTCF pathway. Assuming the prescription is not discontinued, how long may partial fillings continue from the issue date under this special rule?

choices.text: 72 hours
7 days
30 days
60 days
6 months

candidate_texts.stem: A resident pharmacy will close in 20 days. Which timing and transfer statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Delay patient-file transfers until all controlled stock is disposed of.
Send the Board certified written notice at least 14 days before closure.
Identify patients served in the preceding 90 days and attempt notice at least 14 days before closure.
Handle requested file transfers promptly enough to avoid delaying therapy.
Within 14 days after closure, submit original credentials and the controlled-substance disposition attestation.

candidate_texts.stem: An agent collecting a Schedule IV prescription for a housebound Massachusetts patient has no government identification with her. The pharmacist believes refusing would cause the patient real hardship. Which statements about dispensing without a Customer Identifier are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The pharmacist's belief about hardship is by itself sufficient.
The reason for dispensing without an identifier must be documented.
A regular patient known to the pharmacy is outside the requirement.
The agent must print her name and address and sign for the dispensing.
The requirement reaches Schedule VI dispensings on the same terms.

candidate_texts.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is revising the pickup procedure. One prescription is for an ordinary Schedule VI drug that has not been designated by the Commissioner for the additional-drug identification requirement. Another is for a drug that has received that formal designation. Which statements correctly describe the Customer Identifier rule? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The designated additional drug is within the Customer Identifier rule even though it is not described as a Schedule II through V drug.
Every Schedule VI dispensing is within the rule because Massachusetts calls Schedule VI a controlled-substance schedule.
Dispensing a controlled substance in Schedule II, III, IV, or V is within the rule's stated scope.
The ordinary Schedule VI drug is not brought within the rule merely by its Schedule VI classification.
A familiar customer may receive a covered drug without identification or the documented hardship procedure.

candidate_texts.stem:
A agent arrives to collect an ordinary PMP-reportable prescription subject to the customer-identifier rule. The actual recipient presents a valid acceptable government-issued identifier. The pharmacist has not established a serious-hardship basis. The required printed name, address, and signature are not recorded. No delivery/refill-specific waiver applies.

Which handling of the identifier requirement matches these facts? Select ONE answer.

choices.text: Inspect and record the applicable identifier for the actual recipient.
Use the documented hardship pathway with the required recipient record.
Complete the missing hardship documentation and recipient record before relying on that exception.
The facts do not establish an identifier exception; obtain an acceptable identifier or establish another applicable lawful route.

candidate_texts.stem: At the patient's request, one DEA-registered retail pharmacy is asked to transfer an unfilled electronic MS Contin prescription to another DEA-registered retail pharmacy. Which pathway applies?

choices.text: Print the electronic prescription and fax the image.
Transfer it repeatedly while no quantity has been dispensed.
Have technicians at both pharmacies complete the transfer without pharmacist communication.
Use a one-time pharmacist-to-pharmacist electronic transfer after confirming state permission and federal compliance.
Treat the transaction as a Schedule II refill at the receiving pharmacy.

candidate_texts.stem: During prospective legal review, an unfilled electronic Librium prescription has already been transferred once at the patient's request. The patient now seeks a second transfer. What is the result?

choices.text: Permit a second transfer because no dose has been dispensed.
Print and fax it so the next transaction is no longer electronic.
Return it to the original pharmacy and treat that return as a refill.
Allow another transfer when the patient consents in writing.
Do not transfer it a second time under the federal one-time electronic controlled-prescription rule.

candidate_texts.stem:

Which response best fits these facts? Select ONE answer.

choices.text: Convert the prescription to a fax between the pharmacies to satisfy the electronic-transfer rule.
Ask a certified technician to substitute for the required licensed-pharmacist communication.
Do not use this pathway with a prior initial electronic transfer; resolve the defect or use another lawful authorization route.
Apply the real-time-database refill exception to remove every initial-transfer condition.

candidate_texts.stem: A patient asks Pharmacy B to obtain a Massachusetts warfarin prescription from Pharmacy A. The prescription was issued 10 months ago and has three authorized refills remaining. choices.text: The pharmacies should act on the patient’s transfer request in a timely manner rather than impose a blanket no-transfer rule.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions, and the remaining authorized refills may be transferred while the prescription is within the one-year limit.
A certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI prescription transfer when the pharmacist on duty approves the activity.
Massachusetts requires the transferring pharmacy to charge the patient a transfer fee before releasing the prescription.
The transfer is barred solely because the prescription is more than six months old, even though it was issued less than one year ago.

candidate_texts.stem: During a required controlled-substance inventory, a pharmacist reviews several opened containers. Which counting decisions comply with the federal inventory rule? Select all that apply.

Decline further dispensing; require a new lawful prescription.
